title: The Manhattan Grid
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Commissioner's Plan of 1811, which laid out Manhattan's street grid north of Houston Street. They cover why Manhattan's grid works for navigation, criticism of the grid from figures like Walt Whitman and Edith Wharton, earlier grids (Indus Valley, Hippodamus, Spanish Law of the Indies, Philadelphia), the 1790s common lands survey by Casimir Gerk, the 1807 state law creating three commissioners (Gouverneur Morris, John Rutherford, Simeon De Witt), the plan's copying of Gerk's survey, its arbitrary street widths, its lack of public green space, the displacement of residents and lawsuits, and the early apartment building Stuyvesant's Folly. The episode closes with listener mail about narcolepsy resources.

segments.title: Opening banter and grid primer
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the New York City episode and the book A City on a Grid by Gerald Keppel. They explain how Manhattan's numbered streets and avenues form a near-perfect grid north of Houston, how even and odd streets run, and how the grid is both easy to navigate and criticized as soulless.

segments.title: Criticism of the grid
segments.summary: The hosts quote critics of the grid, including Walt Whitman and Edith Wharton, and mention architecture critic Peter Mark Huse and architects who praised it as pragmatic.

segments.title: Earlier grid cities
segments.summary: Grids are traced to the Indus Valley city of Mohenjo-daro, Greek planner Hippodamus, Spanish colonial towns under the Law of the Indies, and William Penn's Philadelphia.

segments.title: Pre-grid Manhattan and the common lands survey
segments.summary: Lower Manhattan's organic street layout is contrasted with the planned grid. In the 1780s the city sold common lands to pay Revolutionary War debts, and surveyor Casimir Gerk divided them into five-acre parcels using a 66-foot chain.

segments.title: The 1807 law and the three commissioners
segments.summary: In 1807 the New York State Legislature gave three commissioners absolute authority over street layout: Gouverneur Morris, John Rutherford, and Simeon De Witt. The hosts describe each man's background and their weak performance on the commission.

segments.title: How the 1811 plan was built and its flaws
segments.summary: The commission copied Gerk's grid, added avenues and numbered streets, and set arbitrary widths for avenues and cross streets. Avenue spacing differed between east and west sides. The report justified the plan as having the least inconvenience. The plan left little public green space and relied on the rivers as parks.

segments.title: Displacement, lawsuits, and Stuyvesant's Folly
segments.summary: The plan required tearing down buildings and filling ponds and marshes, prompting lawsuits and opposition such as Clement Clark Moore's pamphlet. Growth filled the grid slowly, and the 1869 Stuyvesant's Folly apartment building was an early example of apartment living.

segments.title: Closing and next topics
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up New York topics and joke about covering Des Moines next.

segments.title: Listener mail on narcolepsy
segments.summary: Listener Brooke writes about her son Owen's narcolepsy and recommends Julie Flygare's book Wide Awake and Dreaming and the organizations Project Sleep and Voices of Narcolepsy. The hosts plan to send Owen a package.
